title: Bowing to the word
hookLine: people bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and may leave an offering
last: REHRAS · SOHILA · BANI · YOUR NITNEM · GURDWARA · THE OPEN DOOR.

cards: You've left your shoes at the rack. Your head is covered. You step into the main hall, the darbar, and it's bigger and brighter than you expected.
Carpets or white sheets cover the floor. People sit cross-legged. Harmonium, tabla, voices singing.
And at the far end, raised up under a canopy, wrapped in beautiful cloth, is a book. One by one, people walk up the middle of the room toward it, kneel, and touch their foreheads to the floor.
What are they doing, and what are they bowing to?

teach.b: It's called matha tekna. Matha is the forehead; tekna means to rest, to lean it down. Resting your forehead before the Guru.
And the Guru here is the Guru Granth Sahib.
Sikh tradition tells that in 1708, before he died, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, declared there would be no more human Gurus after him.
The Guru would be the word itself, the scripture, alongside the community, the Khalsa Panth. So Sikhs bowing in the gurdwara aren't bowing to paper and ink, and not to an idol.
They're bowing to the Guru's word, the living teacher, present in the room.

teach.h: THE AISLE, THE GOLAK, THE BOW.
teach.b: How it's done: people walk slowly up the central aisle, often with hands folded. Many place an offering before the Granth: money in the box called the golak, food for the langar kitchen, or nothing at all.
Then they kneel, touch their forehead to the floor, step back and sit among the sangat, usually taking care not to sit with their feet or back toward the Guru Granth Sahib.
The offering isn't a fee. The gurdwara runs on the community's giving, and the golak pays for the langar and the building, but nobody checks what you gave. Visitors aren't required to bow.
Many do, as a sign of respect, the way you'd stand when someone honored walks into a room. Others simply sit quietly, and that's fine too. The point is the humility.
The head, raised all day, goes down before a word bigger than any of us.

how: On entering the main hall of a gurdwara, Sikhs walk up to the Guru Granth Sahib, may place an offering of money or food, and kneel to touch their forehead to the floor before sitting with the sangat; visitors are welcome to bow or simply sit.

touching the feet of an elder to show respect

games.q: you're visiting a gurdwara for the first time. people are walking up to bow before the Guru Granth Sahib. what are you expected to do?
o: you must bow and leave an offering.
bow if you wish, or simply sit quietly.
leave the hall until the bowing is over.
games.why: visitors aren't required to bow. many do as a sign of respect; sitting quietly is welcome too.

practice: If you're able, kneel and rest your forehead on the floor, on your folded hands or on a table in front of you; if kneeling isn't possible, just lower your head, and stay there for a few breaths.
Notice what it feels like to put the head, the busiest part of you, lower than your heart. If you pray, bow to the Guru's word; if not, bow to whatever you owe gratitude today, then sit up slowly.

wordCard.voice: Matha tekna. Resting the forehead to the floor before the Guru Granth Sahib: bowing to the word, not to paper.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: resting the forehead down, the bow before the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: bow to the word. The head goes down; the word stays high. One hundred forty days, and counting.
